questions.label: Is the software supplied to the user and run on the user's own system (not only used remotely through a browser)?
questions.guidance: Apps, desktop programs and browser extensions installed by the user are products. A web application or website used only through a browser is not, unless it supports a function of a product (see the remote data processing questions).

questions.label: Is this release unfinished software (alpha, beta, release candidate) made available only for testing?
questions.guidance: Allowed without complying only for the time needed to test and gather feedback, with a visible notice that it does not comply and is not for other purposes. A normal release with some features labelled beta does not qualify: see the next question.

questions.label: Does this normal release include features labelled beta, preview or experimental?
questions.guidance: The release as a whole is placed on the market, so these features need the same risk assessment and essential requirements as any other. Ship them in a separate tester-only build, or disabled with their risks already assessed.

questions.label: Does the product rely on data processing at a distance (cloud, back-end, on-premises server), outside the user's own environment?
Would any of the product's functions stop working without that remote processing?
questions.guidance: Functions include commands, synchronisation, onboarding, configuration, update distribution and identity management. Telemetry collected only for statistics or future development does not count.

questions.label: Is that remote processing software designed and developed by you or specifically for you?
questions.guidance: Your own code running on rented infrastructure or a platform (IaaS, PaaS) counts. A third-party SaaS application you only license does not, but its risks still belong in your risk assessment.

questions.label: Does the product include remote data processing solutions?
Is this hardware supplied as a spare part to repair or maintain an identified product already on the market?
questions.guidance: The repair purpose should be clear from the supply, e.g. the order names the product, or it goes through after-sales channels. Being technically usable as a replacement is not enough.

questions.label: Is the spare part identical to the component it replaces in everything relevant to security (algorithms, protocols, cryptography, access control)?

questions.guidance: Pick by the product's core functionality: its main purpose, without which it would not meet its intended purpose. Ancillary functions and integrated components (e.g. an operating system inside a phone) do not change it. A product that substantially exceeds or falls short of a category is not in it. Modules also sold separately are classified separately. Exactly one choice applies. Category descriptions: Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/2392.

questions.label: Does the product hold an EU type-examination certificate covering cybersecurity under the Radio Equipment Directive's delegated act or the Machinery Regulation?
questions.guidance: It counts as evidence for the risks it covers until 11 June 2028, not beyond, and not for risks it does not cover.

questions.label: How long is the product expected to be in use?
questions.guidance: Consider reasonable user expectations, the nature of the product, hardware durability, comparable products and the support periods of integrated components.

questions.label: When does the support period (security updates and vulnerability handling) end?
questions.guidance: At least five years from placing on the market, unless the product is expected to be used for less; longer when it is expected to be used longer. Users must be told the end date (at least month and year) at purchase.

requirements.label: Design, develop and produce the product to ensure cybersecurity appropriate to its risks
Place the product on the market without known exploitable vulnerabilities
Ship a secure-by-default configuration, with the possibility to reset to the original state
Make vulnerabilities fixable through security updates, automatic by default with an opt-out where applicable
Protect against unauthorised access (authentication, identity and access management) and report possible unauthorised access
Protect the confidentiality of stored, transmitted and processed data, e.g. by encryption
Protect the integrity of data, commands, programs and configuration, and report corruption
Process only data that is adequate, relevant and limited to the intended purpose
Protect the availability of essential functions, including resilience against denial of service
Minimise the product's negative impact on the availability of other devices or networks
Limit attack surfaces, including external interfaces
Reduce the impact of incidents with exploitation mitigation mechanisms
Record and monitor security-relevant internal activity, with a user opt-out
Let users securely remove all data and settings permanently, and transfer data securely
Identify and document vulnerabilities and components, including a software bill of materials of at least top-level dependencies
Remediate vulnerabilities without delay, with security updates separate from feature updates where feasible
Apply effective and regular security tests and reviews
Publicly disclose fixed vulnerabilities once an update is available
Put in place and enforce a coordinated vulnerability disclosure policy
Facilitate sharing information about vulnerabilities, including a contact address for reports
Distribute updates securely
Disseminate security updates without delay and free of charge, with advisory messages
Carry out a cybersecurity risk assessment, document it and keep it up to date
Exercise due diligence on integrated third-party components
Report vulnerabilities in integrated components to their maintainer and share fixes
Determine a support period of at least five years, or the expected use time if shorter
State the end date of the support period at purchase, at least month and year
Provide the information and instructions to the user in Annex II
Draw up the technical documentation in Annex VII and keep it up to date
Carry out the applicable conformity assessment procedure before placing on the market
Draw up the EU declaration of conformity
Affix the CE marking
Keep the technical documentation and declaration of conformity for at least 10 years, or the support period if longer
Notify actively exploited vulnerabilities to the coordinating CSIRT and ENISA: early warning within 24 h, notification within 72 h, final report within 14 days after a fix
Notify severe incidents affecting the product's security: early warning within 24 h, notification within 72 h, final report within one month
Inform impacted users about actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents, and about mitigations
Keep the declaration of conformity and technical documentation available to market surveillance authorities and cooperate with them, as mandated
Place only conforming products: check the conformity assessment, technical documentation, CE marking and user information
Indicate your name and contact address on the product, its packaging or documentation
Inform the manufacturer of vulnerabilities, and market surveillance authorities where the risk is significant
Before making the product available, check the CE marking and the manufacturer's and importer's documentation
Inform the manufacturer of vulnerabilities, and market surveillance authorities where the risk is significant
Put in place and document a cybersecurity policy for the free and open-source software you support
Cooperate with market surveillance authorities on request

assessment_routes.label: EU-type examination with conformity to type (modules B and C)

finding_rules.message: Important class I without full harmonised-standard coverage: a third-party conformity assessment (modules B+C, H or EUCC) is required.
Important class II or critical: a third-party conformity assessment is required (critical products may need European cybersecurity certification under a delegated act).
The support period is shorter than the minimum: at least five years, or the whole expected use time if that is shorter.
The support period meets the five-year minimum but is shorter than the expected use time; a longer period is expected for products used longer.
This release is a substantial modification: it is placed on the market anew, needs a new conformity assessment (focused on the changed parts) and its own support period.
Unfinished software may be made available without complying only for the time needed for testing, with a visible notice that it does not comply.
Preview or beta features in a normal release are part of the product placed on the market: include them in the risk assessment and essential requirements, or move them to a separate test build.
An open debug interface in shipped units is attack surface.
The same default password on every unit is not a secure-by-default configuration.
Without an update mechanism, vulnerabilities cannot be addressed through security updates.

A design from before 11 December 2027 needs no redesign if a current risk assessment shows adequate measures, but conformity assessment, CE marking and vulnerability handling still apply.
The existing certificate counts as evidence for the risks it covers until 11 June 2028; other risks must be assessed under the CRA.
Outside the CRA, but national rules on classified information apply instead (e.g. security accreditation); check with the national security authority.
The remote data processing solution is part of the product: cover it in the risk assessment, essential requirements and reporting.
